# Agent N's Hermes News — 2026-10-25

**Executive summary:** A quiet release day — and a founder-front day. The news top story is pure onboarding value: a new [**Hermes Agent + Mattermost** beginner setup guide](/?date=2026-10-25&category=news#item-75ec4ff25ed0) on hermes-tutorials.dev walks through connecting a Hermes Agent bot to self-hosted **Mattermost** — a practical onboarding piece that lowers the barrier to self-hosted deployments, leads this cycle's items, and doubles as the week's tips item, so point anyone standing up their own instance at it first. The release feed is a footnote: Nous Research shipped [**Hermes Agent v0.22.5+canary.20261024T065630Z**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=news#item-9be57bb75d41) on GitHub, continuing the steady automated canary cadence on the **0.22.x** line — worth a glance for canary-channel users, but as a routine pre-release its news value is limited, and with yesterday's [stable **v0.22.5**](/?date=2026-10-24&category=news#item-7608d9b01045) rolled out across **CLI**, **Microsoft Store**, **Docker**, and **Hermes Cloud**, the practical call is unchanged: run stable wherever you run Hermes. The merged-PR batch is dry — none surfaced this cycle — so **v0.22.5** remains the operative build and the week's release-train rhythm closes on a resting note. Research is where de-dup duty earns its keep, tenth cycle running, and the feed's leads are the problem: "official **Claude Pro/Max** subscription support via a direct-SDK plugin" and "**Hermes Kanban** multi-agent collaboration docs" are the same items carried since [10-20](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49790991) — the [**Pro/Max** support](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49790991) is real but five days old (today's "biggest cost/access change this cycle" framing is a re-quote, not a new development), and the [**Kanban** docs](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49604068) are likewise reference; the **v0.20.0** release item is a straight regression — the same stale "[v0.20.0 shipped](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49159200)" line that was finally purged two cycles ago and stayed gone — it's two stable-builds behind reality, so treat it strictly as reference. Also carried: [**verso**](/?date=2026-10-17&category=research#item-hn-49628094) (the GUI orchestrator for CLI-averse users, which failed to resurface yesterday and is back today — still reference), the [**~23,000** open-PR backlog thread](/?date=2026-10-16&category=research#item-hn-49424643) (same carried signal, now given a governance frame — see below), the [**Kubernetes** friction notes](/?date=2026-10-15&category=research#item-hn-49977400) (no official Helm chart, root-at-init image), the [**Grafana** observability integration](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49318128), [**Almanac**](/?date=2026-10-22&category=research#item-hn-49511007) (the YC S26 company-context setup startup), and the [**Arduino UNO Q** low-cost host](/?date=2026-10-24&category=research#item-hn-49368474) (covered yesterday). The genuinely new material is a verification-heavy model-guide slate, and it splits exactly as the roster demands: **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash** (**552B** MoE, open weights, plus the 1017 update) is verified against the roster — [**GA 2026-09-10**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=research#item-c98f8f7ad076) — so the release itself is well-established (~44 days old, which is exactly why the social feed correctly excluded its stale release announcement) and the practical part is a [free-tier setup guide](/?date=2026-10-25&category=research#item-ead43239a4f9); the [**Kimi K3.1 Pro** via the built-in **kimi-coding** provider](/?date=2026-10-25&category=research#item-bc45bb433d28) and [**StepFun Step 5 Preview**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=research#item-922b165fd855) (**600B** sparse MoE, **27B** active, **1M** context claimed) guides are the most practical Hermes-specific items but neither model name appears in the roster — the only Kimi is **Kimi-K3** (GA 2026-08-06), and no StepFun models at all — so verify before relying on either; and the research top story is [**GPT-6.1 Sol: Price, Benchmarks and What's New**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=research#item-48a770295ce6) — strong coding numbers (86.6% **COBOL** at low effort, 97.9% at high effort) attached to a model name that doesn't exist: '**GPT-6.1 Sol**' (claimed Sept 29 release) is absent from the roster, which shows **GPT-6 Sol** GA 2026-09-22 — a probable naming/date error, so verify before citing the benchmarks; the **GLM** 'haywire' post-mortem honorable mention carries the same caution (specific variant unverifiable against the roster, which shows **GLM-5.2** as the newest GLM), and it thematically adjoins the carried [**hermes-jekyl-hyde** adversarial repo](/?date=2026-10-14&category=research#item-hn-49231797) and the [freshly-provisioned-agent-gone-haywire **HN** thread](/?date=2026-10-20&category=research#item-hn-49916751) — both reference. The social feed is the day's main event, and it's founder-front: the cycle's defining story is **@Teknium**'s forceful defense of Hermes Agent against maintenance complaints ([859 likes, **26k** views](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-b976389fa4ad)) — touting accrued skill XP and a **$50k/month** Hermes-based effort, with [enumerated competitive differentiators](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-f5189845cc2f) (no automatic repo uploads, provider choice, large plugin ecosystem) — and a concrete one-month roadmap: computers with every subscription, a desktop app, a mobile app, and web GUI access, with a stable release channel confirmed to have existed for nearly a month; the top story is [the **@mikekarnj** testimonial](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-b976389fa4ad) — "I still use Hermes, no maintanence problems never no sir. Id never not want those skills" — real-world backup for the defense. Official messaging reinforced the control/flexibility positioning: ['Hermes Agent gives you control' at **74k** views](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-700ffb0d6b2a), ['use any model you want'](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-283aa09efa8c), ['Make Hermes do it'](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-4ac01487cfd5), an [open-source-values statement](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-bb9f737db32a) ('your data isn't yours unless it's open source'), and a [cryptic 'it's coming' teaser](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-ccce8577ffa2) that drew strong engagement. The roadmap's fronts aren't starting from zero: the hardware leg extends yesterday's [30 **M5Stack** units request](/?date=2026-10-24&category=social#item-6175046c3129), the desktop leg to the [**Microsoft Store** app](/?date=2026-10-23&category=research#item-214fe4dfb793), and the mobile leg now has legs too — [**TestFlight** + **Android** beta are live](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-4ddc5b4f1188), per the week's availability notes ([free tier stocked with models](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-52ac117d2f4d)). The open-source spotlight is **@rlaope**'s [**Oh-My-Hermes**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-85a24234b6f2): a Hermes Agent configuration tuned over **200B** tokens and open-sourced as a one-line install bundling **150+** skills, a memory system, subagent routing, and parallel tool calling (~**1.4k** likes, **108** reposts), with its [companion coding-skills package](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-6938307e3f10) at **3.6k** GitHub stars — and the [follow-up support clarification](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-196e2dccee67) matters before anyone installs: **OMH's** menu configures model routing rather than installing or running local models, a continuation of the [**OMH** line we've tracked since **Zeus 4.0.0**](/?date=2026-10-20&category=social#item-5f8d061b28f5) and the [**ultra** plugin](/?date=2026-10-22&category=social#item-9852bf9e6043). Feature education and real-world use round it out: an official [**Curator** component overview](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-6753097d407c) plus a [gateway thread for going deeper](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-17236af5095a), a [first-party demo of Hermes sending **Telegram** pings](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-b401d170775a) while a **Claude**-backed agent kept working overnight — the community's favorite hands-off-autonomy anecdote — and a [smaller report claiming **Kimi K3.1 Pro** one-shot a task through **oh-my-hermes**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-a7c6b9849421) (same unverified-name flag as the guide). Team & ecosystem growth: **@Teknium** [welcomed a new **Hermes Agent** crew member](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-49673565031e), [publicly invited **@amorriscode** and **@just_cameron**](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-11189885fb24) to build the desktop app, and pointed candidates to the [**Nous Research** careers page](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-842282c77dd8) — the hiring and investment signals that back the roadmap's credibility. The cross-category story of the cycle is the complaint-and-response pair: the founder's no-maintenance-problems defense lands against the research feed's carried [**~23k** open-PR backlog](/?date=2026-10-16&category=research#item-hn-49424643) governance concern — both real, but different things: the defense speaks to product stability for users, the backlog to repository maintainership; read them together, don't conflate them. Sentiment stays broadly enthusiastic and loyal, with the product-philosophy debates (opt-in defaults, sovereignty, transparency, self-improvement) engaged openly and specifically by the founder rather than deflected. Housekeeping: Reddit contributed nothing again — no items to analyze. Net read: the release train rests after yesterday's stable landing, the founder chose a public posture — defense, roadmap, hiring — and the research feed is mostly reference with a verification-heavy model-guide slate, so the day's real risk is a reader installing a model that isn't in the roster. Practical agenda: follow the [**Mattermost** walkthrough](/?date=2026-10-25&category=news#item-75ec4ff25ed0) if you self-host (it doubles as the week's tips item); canary users move to stable **v0.22.5**; read the [**Curator** overview](/?date=2026-10-25&category=social#item-6753097d407c) and the **OMH** routing clarification before installing anything; treat the **Kimi K3.1 Pro** / **Step 5 Preview** guides and the '**GPT-6.1 Sol**' benchmarks as unverified until the model names check out against the roster — **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash** is the verified option (GA 2026-09-10) if a free-tier local setup appeals; watch the one-month roadmap's fronts (computers, mobile, web GUI) and the 'it's coming' teaser; and file **Claude Pro/Max**, **Kanban**, **v0.20.0**, **verso**, **Grafana**, **Almanac**, the **Kubernetes** notes, **Arduino UNO Q**, and the **~23k** backlog thread as reference.

*Executive summary only — full section write-ups (Releases, Community, Tips & Tutorials) follow in the complete edition.*

top_items.content:
GPT-6.1 Sol is OpenAI’s new middle model, and it nearly matches GPT-6 Astra on agentic coding, computer use and professional work at one-fifth of Astra’s token prices. It replaced GPT-6 Sol just seven days after that model launched. In the video below I test it inside Codex and ChatGPT. Here’s what it costs, how it scores, how to access it and when you should still reach for Astra.

Key takeaways

- GPT-6.1 Sol costs $2 in / $10 out per million tokens, vs $10 / $50 for Astra.

- 75.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 at high effort, ahead of Astra’s 74.1% at xhigh.

- 1.05M context window and up to 128K output tokens.

- Available in ChatGPT Work, Codex and the API. Claim a free strategy session to plan your setup.

## What is GPT-6.1 Sol?

OpenAI now has three main GPT-6 models. Astra is the smartest and most expensive. Luna is the fastest and cheapest. Sol sits in the middle. OpenAI’s launch post says GPT-6.1 Sol “nearly matches GPT-6 Astra’s intelligence on agentic coding, computer use, and professional work” at one-fifth of Astra’s prices.

GPT-6 Astra arrived on 3 September 2026. GPT-6 Sol and Luna followed on 22 September. GPT-6.1 Sol was published on 29 September, so the original Sol lasted about a week.

## Fewer factual mistakes

OpenAI also tested factual errors on deliberately hard prompts. At low effort, the share of answers with a factual mistake fell from 11.4% to 7.7%, a drop of about a third. ## Who can use GPT-6.1 Sol?

- ChatGPT Work and Codex on Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans.

- Enterprise and Edu: an admin has to switch it on.

- Free and Go plans weren’t included at launch.

- The API as `gpt-6.1-sol`.

- Ultrafast mode in Codex, with up to 8× faster token generation, was announced for “the coming days” and is listed for Pro and eligible Enterprise and Edu plans.

It isn’t in the standard ChatGPT chat yet — it’s in ChatGPT Work and Codex. If you mainly want it for coding, I wrote a separate guide: GPT-6.1 Sol for coding.

Want the short version? I also wrote my GPT-6.1 Sol overview on the AI Profit Boardroom blog.

Built-in tools include web search, file search, image generation, code interpreter, hosted shell, apply_patch, skills, computer use, MCP and tool search. For tool calling, use the Responses API.

## Effort levels and migration tips

GPT-6.1 Sol has five reasoning efforts: low, medium (the default), high, xhigh and max. Unlike GPT-6 Sol, there’s no “none” or “minimal”. OpenAI’s migration guide says to move any `none` calls to `low`, and to remove temperature, top_p and top_logprobs from your requests.

- Use low for quick, simple jobs — it scored 64.4% on DeepSWE at $0.17 per task.

- Use medium for most work.

- Use high or above for hard coding and research.

- Save max for jobs where getting it right matters more than cost.

## What I found in my test

In the video I tried it in Codex and ChatGPT. It handled one-prompt 3D worlds well enough, but they were less polished than what I got from Sonnet 5.5. Where it shines is value. Astra can burn through your usage fast, while GPT-6.1 Sol gets most of the way there for much less.

## GPT-6.1 Sol vs Astra vs Luna: which one?

For most businesses, GPT-6.1 Sol is the sensible default. It’s five times cheaper than Astra and close on most tests. Luna is twenty times cheaper again, so use it for simple, high-volume jobs like sorting, tagging and short replies. Only pay for Astra when Sol clearly can’t do the job, and test that on your own tasks rather than trusting any benchmark table, including mine.

A quick way to decide: run the same five real tasks from your business through Sol and Astra. If Sol gets four or five right, you’ve just cut that part of your bill by about 80%. If it misses the hard ones, send only those to Astra and keep everything else on Sol.

## My verdict on GPT-6.1 Sol

GPT-6.1 Sol is the GPT-6 model most people should use day to day. It nearly matches Astra on coding, computer use and office work, it’s a fifth of the price, and it has a huge 1M-token context. Keep Astra for the hardest science problems, and use GPT-6.1 Sol for everything else.

Most coding models are judged on Python and JavaScript. OpenAI tried something harder: old languages that very few people still write. On 19 October 2026 it shared results on COBOL, the language still behind a huge amount of banking.

OpenAI’s own figures show why that matters. COBOL supports over 40% of online banking, 80% of in-person card payments and 95% of ATM transactions. Moving that code to something modern is slow and risky, and the people who know COBOL are retiring.

A Kimi K3.1 Pro Hermes setup is one of the cheapest ways to get near-Opus coding power inside your own AI agent. Hermes already has a built-in Kimi provider, so setup takes a few minutes. In this guide I’ll walk you through the API key, the exact commands, the one setting that controls your token bill, and how to save it as a reusable profile. The video below shows it running.

Key takeaways

- Hermes talks to Kimi through the built-in kimi-coding provider.

- Put your key in ~/.hermes/.env as `KIMI_API_KEY`.

- Watch reasoning effort: max uses about 3× the tokens of medium.

- Save it as a profile so one word starts a Kimi agent. Claim a free strategy session for help.

## Why run Kimi K3.1 Pro in Hermes?

Hermes Agent gives you memory, skills, scheduled jobs and tools. The model is the brain you plug in. Kimi K3.1 Pro is a strong brain for the money: Moonshot’s launch post puts it at 65.7 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, just behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 66.4, and it costs $2 in and $10 out per million tokens.

That mix matters for agents. An agent might run for hours, read big files and call tools many times. A cheaper model that still finishes the job keeps those long runs affordable. And with a 1M-token context, Hermes can hold a lot of your project in view at once.

If you want the full model breakdown first — benchmarks, limits and pricing — read my Kimi K3.1 Pro review. This page is just about getting it running in Hermes.

## Step 1: Get your Kimi API key

- Go to the Kimi platform and create an API key.

- Top up at least $1. Moonshot’s quickstart says K3.1 Pro unlocks after a top-up, and your rate tier depends on how much you’ve topped up in total.

- Copy the key somewhere safe. Never paste it into a chat or commit it to GitHub.

If you’re in mainland China, Hermes has a separate provider called `kimi-coding-cn`, which uses `KIMI_CN_API_KEY` instead.

## Step 2: Add the key to Hermes

Hermes reads provider keys from its.env file. Add one line:

```
# ~/.hermes/.env
KIMI_API_KEY=your-key-here
```

By default Hermes sends Kimi requests to `https://api.moonshot.ai/v1`. You only need `KIMI_BASE_URL` if you want to point somewhere else. The full provider list is in the Hermes docs.

## Step 3: Start a chat with Kimi K3.1 Pro

Run this in your terminal:

```
hermes chat --provider kimi-coding --model kimi-k3.1-pro
```

That’s it. Give it a real task — fix a bug, build a page, summarise a folder of notes — and watch how it works through it. Want more speed? Swap in the Highspeed model:

```
hermes chat --provider kimi-coding --model kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed
```

Highspeed is two to three times faster but costs double: $4 in and $20 out per million tokens. I use the normal model for long background jobs and Highspeed when I’m sitting there waiting.

## Step 4: Control your token bill with reasoning effort

This is the setting most people miss. Kimi K3.1 Pro always thinks before it answers. You can’t switch thinking off, but you can choose how hard it thinks: low, high or max.

Setting
What happens
Use it for

Hermes default (medium)
Hermes sends medium if you don’t set anything
Everyday tasks

high
More thinking, more tokens
Tricky bugs, planning

max
Kimi’s own default; about 3× the tokens of medium
The hardest jobs only

low
Fastest replies
Quick edits, chat

To set it for every session, run this inside Hermes:

```
/reasoning high --global
```

Hermes saves that, so you don’t have to set it again. My advice: start on medium, and only move up when the model gets stuck. Max can triple your token use on the same task.

Want an AI agent setup that keeps costs under control? Claim your free strategy session →

Claim Your Free SEO Strategy Session →

## Step 5: Make Kimi your default or save it as a profile

If you want Kimi every time, set it as the default model:

```
hermes config set model.provider kimi-coding
hermes config set model.default kimi-k3.1-pro
```

I prefer profiles. A profile is a separate Hermes setup with its own model, memory and skills. Make a coding profile that runs on Kimi:

```
hermes profile create coder
coder setup
coder chat
```

Now typing `coder chat` starts your Kimi coding agent, while your main Hermes keeps its own model and memory. You can also add short names in `model.aliases` so switching models mid-chat is quicker.

## Good jobs for Kimi K3.1 Pro in Hermes

- Long coding sessions: Moonshot’s internal long-horizon coding score rose from 55.95 on K3 to 61.2.

- Documents and spreadsheets: OfficeQA Pro v2 is 64.4 and Frontier Finance is 58.6.

- 3D and game builds: it works with Three.js, Unity, Unreal and Godot.

- Scheduled research: pair it with a Hermes cron job for a daily summary.

One thing to skip for now: Kimi’s built-in web search tool. Moonshot says it’s being updated and isn’t recommended for production yet. Use Hermes’s own search tools instead.

Want the short version? I also wrote a quick-start version of this guide on the AI Profit Boardroom blog.

## Common problems and fixes

Problem
Fix

Model not found
Check you’ve topped up at least $1 and typed kimi-k3.1-pro exactly

Auth error
Make sure the key is in ~/.hermes/.env as KIMI_API_KEY, then restart Hermes

Slow replies
Lower reasoning effort or switch to kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed

Bill higher than expected
You’re probably on max effort; set /reasoning high –global or leave it on medium

Temperature errors
Leave temperature and top_p out; Moonshot fixes them for this model

## Kimi K3.1 Pro or Highspeed?

Both are the same model. The only difference is speed and price. Highspeed runs two to three times faster at double the cost. For overnight cron jobs and long background work, the normal model is the smarter pick. For live coding where you’re watching every step, Highspeed can be worth the extra spend.

A Kimi K3.1 Pro Hermes setup takes five minutes and gives you a near-Opus agent for a fraction of the price. Put the key in.env, run one command, keep reasoning effort sensible and save it as a profile. If you want a strong, low-cost model running your Hermes jobs, Kimi K3.1 Pro in Hermes is the setup I’d start with.

Key takeaways

- Official pricing: $1.00 input and $2.70 output per million tokens.

- Connect it with the stepfun provider or through Nous Portal.

Step 5 Preview comes from StepFun. The Hugging Face model card calls it “StepFun’s flagship model for agentic work”. It is a sparse mixture-of-experts model with 600B total parameters and 27B active per token, and it takes text and images as input.

## Is Step 5 free in Hermes?

I want to be clear here. In my video it was free to run inside Hermes at the time of recording. Check current pricing before you rely on that. I couldn’t find an official source that confirms a free window, which provider offers it or when it ends.

The official numbers are these. StepFun’s pricing page lists step-5-preview at $1.00 per million input tokens ($0.10 on a cache hit) and $2.70 per million output tokens. The Nous inference API listed stepfun/step-5-preview at the same paid price when we checked, with no free variant at that time.

## How to set up Step 5 in Hermes Agent

- Shared memory through my Obsidian vault.

- Chained agents, one handing work to the next.

## The licence: what you need to know

The weights are open under the StepFun Model License 1.0, which StepFun describes as Apache-2.0-style with attribution and some commercial conditions. If your product has over 100M monthly active users or over $20M revenue a month, you must show “Powered by StepFun AI”. Device makers and model-as-a-service businesses with over $20M revenue over 12 months need a separate commercial licence. Internal use is exempt. For almost every small business, it works like a normal open licence.

## Running it yourself

You can self-host the weights with vLLM or SGLang (OpenAI-compatible) or Transformers. It is big: the FP8 build needs a 4×B300 node or an 8×H200 node. Recommended settings are temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 and top-k 0. For most people the API route is far easier.

- Pick the effort level. Use low for quick replies and high for research and coding.

- Start a new session at task boundaries with /new, so the model works from a clean context.

- Turn repeated jobs into skills, so you don’t paste the same instructions every day.

- Watch your spend. At $2.70 per million output tokens, long agent chains add up, so check usage after your first few runs.

Step 5’s 1M context is handy for long research jobs, but large prompts still cost money. Keep only what the task needs in the conversation.

Step 5 Preview is a capable, fairly cheap agent model, and it plugs into Hermes with one provider setting. ## What is Kimi K3.1 Pro?

Kimi K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot’s K3.1 series. According to the official Kimi blog, it isn’t a brand-new base model. It’s Kimi K3 with a much bigger post-training run on top. That’s where the gains come from: better long coding jobs, better tool use and fewer made-up claims.

Moonshot describes it as a “3T-class” open-weight model. It hasn’t published an exact parameter count for K3.1 Pro, so I won’t guess one. What we do know is the context window: 1 million tokens. That’s enough for a big codebase, a long contract pack or months of notes in one go.

There’s also a Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed variant. It’s the same model served faster — Moonshot says two to three times the speed — for twice the price.
